ety.text: Old Northern French moverbor. Middle English moven English move From Middle English moven, moeven, meven, borrowed from Old Northern French mover, moveir and Old French mouver, moveir (“to move”) (compare modern French mouvoir from Old French movoir), from Latin movēre (“move; change, exchange, go in or out, quit”), from Proto-Indo-European *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move, drive”). Cognate with Lithuanian mauti (“to push on, rush”), Sanskrit मीवति (mī́vati, “pushes, presses, moves”), Middle Dutch mouwe (“sleeve”).

senses.d: To change place or posture; to go, in any manner, from one place or position to another.
ex: A ship moves rapidly.
I was sitting on the sofa for a long time, feeling too lazy to move.

senses.d: To act; to take action; to begin to act
ex: to move in a matter
Come on guys, let's move: there's work to do!

senses.d: To change residence, for example from one house, town, or state, to another; to go and live at another place; similarly to change the location of another establishment such as a business. See also move out and move in.
ex: I decided to move to the country for a more peaceful life.
They moved closer to work to cut down commuting time.

senses.d: To transport (an item) as part of changing residences.
ex: Before my lease ended, I gave away my old sofa because I didn't want to move it.

senses.d: To cause to change place or posture in any manner; to set in motion; to carry, convey, draw, or push from one place to another
ex: The waves moved the boat up and down.
The horse moves a carriage.

senses.d: To transfer (a piece) from one space or position on the board to another.
ex: She moved the queen closer to the centre of the board.
He rolled a 5 and moved his counter to Boardwalk, the most expensive property on the Monopoly board.

senses.d: To excite to action by the presentation of motives; to rouse by representation, persuasion, or appeal; to influence.
ex: This song moves me to dance.
Seducer of the People, not moved with the Piety of his Life

senses.d: To arouse the feelings or passions of; especially, to excite to tenderness or compassion, to excite (for example, an emotion).
ex: That book really moved me.
When he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them.

senses.d: To propose; to recommend; specifically, to propose formally for consideration and determination, in a deliberative assembly; to submit
ex: I move to repeal the rule regarding obligatory school uniform.
Let me but move one question to your daughter.

senses.d: To mention; to raise (a question); to suggest (a course of action); to lodge (a complaint).
The act of moving; a movement.
ex: A slight move of the tiller, and the boat will go off course.
The drummer Cynthia praised her best friends' dance moves to the music.

senses.d: An act for the attainment of an object; a step in the execution of a plan or purpose.
ex: He made another move towards becoming a naturalized citizen.

senses.d: A formalized or practiced action used in athletics, dance, physical exercise, self-defense, hand-to-hand combat, etc.
ex: She always gets spontaneous applause for that one move.
He can win a match with that one move.

senses.d: The event of changing one's residence.
ex: The move into my fiancé's house took two long days.
They were pleased about their move to the country.

senses.d: A change in strategy.
ex: I am worried about our boss's move.
It was a smart move to bring on a tall striker to play against the smaller defenders.

senses.d: A transfer, a change from one employer to another.
The act of moving a token on a gameboard from one position to another according to the rules of the game.
ex: The best move of the game was when he sacrificed his rook in order to gain better possession.
It's your move! Roll the dice!

senses.d: A round, in which each player has a turn.
ex: You can win in three moves if you do that.

senses.d: Within the Minimalist Program, a fundamental operation of syntactic construction
